newsitem.title: FRANCE: France renews call for U.S. troops in Zaire force.
newsitem.headline: France renews call for U.S. troops in Zaire force.

text.p: France on Wednesday again urged the United States to contribute troops to a multinational peace force intended to aid refugees in eastern Zaire.
"It would be unbelievable to us that a great democracy like the United States would not be moved by a human tragedy of this magnitude," Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said.

Despite the return home to Rwanda of hundreds of thousands of the refugees that the peace force was intended to help, Rummelhardt told a routine ministry press briefing that Paris was still preparing to send soldiers to the region as part of a multinational force and said Washington should do the same.
He reiterated France's belief that Americans should make up a third of the force, with European and African soliders making up the remaining two-thirds.

As refugees streamed back into Rwanda, President Bill Clinton said the United States had made no final decision on involvement of U.S. forces in relief efforts. U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said Washington was instead preparing for a military air relief operation.
Britain said the multinational force was still probably needed since international agencies have said the situation in central Africa was still critical.

Rummelhardt said French preparations were continuing "because, despite the encouraging signs, the humanitarian problem remains. It is a very big problem. The international community cannot turn its back".

"The humanitarian problem remains enormous, regardless of what others may have said in recent days," Minister for Urgent Humanitarian Action Xavier Emmanuelli told deputies during parliamentary questions on Wednesday.

"France will do all it can to help these people who are in distress and to draw the attention of the world community to their fate," said Emmanuelli, who had just returned from an evaluation mission to Zaire and Rwanda.

Rwanda's predominantly Tutsi government has objected to French troops in the region, accusing France of being partisan after it sent troops to Rwanda in 1994 to help stop Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
It charges that Paris used the intervention to help protect Hutus responsible for instigating the mass killings.
Kigali apparently fears that French forces, once in the region, might protect Hutu rebels in the zone or act against Tutsi rebels who have been fighting Zairean forces.
But Rummelhardt insisted that its presence would be purely for humanitarian reasons. "France is not pursuing any national interest," the spokesman said.

French President Jacques Chirac said in Tokyo on Tuesday that troops were still required in the region to assure that the Goma and Bukavu regions were secure and to protect airfields and relief convoys.
